title: When Schools Ban AI, What Exactly Are They Banning
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill takes the growing wave of institutional AI bans and asks what such announcements actually prohibit once they meet the software schools already run. Starting from a colleague's reading of the MIT ad hoc committee report, he observes that MIT and Sydney reject blanket restrictions and detector-style silver bullets, but that a fast-moving anti-AI movement is pushing in the opposite direction. He surveys the specific policies: New York City's grade-banded prohibition with teacher and accessibility carve-outs, Los Angeles restricting student access across all grades, the University of Chicago Social Sciences Core going analog, UC Berkeley Law defaulting to prohibition, and Rutgers pausing Canvas IgniteAI features. His central move is to replace the product-level question with a functional taxonomy of five things AI can do in an educational context, from making material accessible to evaluating the student, and to show that the same feature can shift categories depending on use. He then walks through LMS and third-party examples, zyBooks, Zoom, Wooclap, to show how much AI processing happens without a student ever opening a chatbot. Hill concludes that the MIT report and the Sydney green paper, whatever their gaps, at least tell an academic technology team which activity is at issue, who can authorize an exception, and what conditions must be supported, which is more than a moratorium announcement can do.
points: Hill argues the useful policy question is not whether a product contains AI but what work the AI performs, and he sorts uses into five functions: making material accessible, preparing instruction, coaching the student, performing the student's work, and evaluating the student.

He notes that New York City's guidance bars student-facing generative AI through eighth grade while preserving teacher instructional use and accessibility exceptions, whereas Los Angeles restricted student access across all grades pending review.

Embedded LMS features complicate enforcement: Canvas study tools, D2L's Lumi, and Blackboard's rubric checks each straddle several of the five functions, so buying an LMS now means buying policy decisions.
Tools like Zoom AI notes and Wooclap's facilitation features process student work without the student ever opening a chatbot, which leaves restrictions framed around direct student use unresolved.

Hill holds up the MIT committee report and the University of Sydney green paper as better starting points because they name the activity, the authorizer, and the conditions rather than treating the presence of AI as decisive.
quotes: The highest-profile AI bans come from the K-12 world, but given the social contagion nature of this movement, they are relevant to higher education.

NYC is introducing restrictions on particular uses of generative AI, with different rules for students and staff. This does not mean every piece of software containing something its vendor calls AI is no longer allowed.
I, however, find it more useful to ask what work the AI performs in an educational context.
These categories describe use cases. The same product can appear in several rows, and the same feature can change categories depending on how it is used.
The direction is clear, however: buying an LMS increasingly means buying a collection of embedded AI functions that require different policy decisions.
A policy against AI grading might not be clear about whether it also restricts AI-assisted assessment design. Calling the whole product “AI-powered” does not answer that question.
Both MIT and Sydney give an academic technology team something to work with: the relevant activity, who can authorize it, and the conditions that need to be supported.
Otherwise, “we banned AI” tells us more about the announcement than about what will happen in course activities.
